claim: The study used 50 Drosophila and related species, including 46 Drosophila species, 3 Scaptodrosophila species, and 1 Chymomyza species.
source: In this study, 46 Drosophila species, as well as three Scaptodrosophila species and one Chymomyza species were either obtained from the National Drosophila Species Stock Center (NDSSC) or were gifts from various colleagues.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Desiccation resistance varied across the 50 species with desert-dwelling species from the repleta group showing the highest desiccation resistance (e.g., D. mojavensis males: 58.2 ± 4.7 hr).
source: Desiccation resistance varied across these 50 species with desert-dwelling species from the repleta group showing the highest desiccation resistance (e.g., D. mojavensis males: 58.2 ± 4.7 hr) and species from melanogaster group showing the lowest desiccation resistance (e.g., D. mauritiana males: 2.7 ± 0.2 hr) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistent with the findings of previous research (Kellermann et al., 2012; Matzkin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Species from the melanogaster group showed the lowest desiccation resistance (e.g., D. mauritiana males: 2.7 ± 0.2 hr).
source: Desiccation resistance varied across these 50 species with desert-dwelling species from the repleta group showing the highest desiccation resistance (e.g., D. mojavensis males: 58.2 ± 4.7 hr) and species from melanogaster group showing the lowest desiccation resistance (e.g., D. mauritiana males: 2.7 ± 0.2 hr) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistent with the findings of previous research (Kellermann et al., 2012; Matzkin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: GC–MS analyses detected five types of CHCs: linear alkanes (n-alkanes), methyl-branched alkanes (mbCHCs), monoenes, dienes, and trienes.
source: GC–MS analyses of the CHCs in these 50 species detected five types of CHCs with different carbon-chain lengths and quantities, including linear alkanes (n-alkanes), methyl-branched alkanes (mbCHCs; the methyl branch is on the second carbon), monoenes (with one double bond), dienes (with two double bonds), and trienes (with three double bonds) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on GC-MS experimental data described in the Results section.

claim: n-Alkanes have the highest melting temperatures among CHC types.
source: Among them, n-alkanes have the highest melting temperature, followed by mbCHCs , monoenes, and dienes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about CHC chemical properties and is also illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: n-Alkanes were only present in species from the melanogaster group.
source: n-Alkanes, which have the highest melting temperatures, were only present in species from the melanogaster group, some of which have the lowest desiccation resistance among the species tested in this study.
evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Trienes were only present in eight species in low-to-moderate quantities.
source: Trienes, which have the lowest melting temperatures, were only present in eight species in low-to-moderate quantities.
evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: mbCHCs, monoenes, and dienes were observed in most species tested in the study.
source: The other three types of CHCs, the mbCHCs, monoenes, and dienes, were observed in most species tested in our study.
evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Body weight is positively correlated with desiccation resistance (Females: r = 0.4, p < 0.001; Males: r = 0.5, p < 0.001).
source: Our initial analyses showed a significant positive correlation (Females: r = 0.4, p < 0.001; Males: r = 0.5, p < 0.001) between body weight and desiccation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on Pearson correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Total amount of CHCs is positively correlated with body weight (Female: r = 0.7, p < 0.001; Male: r = 0.7, p < 0.001).
source: We also found a significant positive correlation between body weight and total amount of CHCs (Female: r = 0.7, p < 0.001; Male: r = 0.7, p < 0.001) (Figure 3B), suggesting that variation in the body weight (or size) of different species may be a confound in determining the relationship between CHC quantity and desiccation resistance.
evidence: This is based on Pearson correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CHCs account for 0.02–0.5% of the total body weight of different species.
source: This shows that CHCs account for 0.02–0.5% of the total body weight of different species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on normalization of CHC quantity by body weight shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no correlation between normalized CHC quantity and desiccation resistance in males (p = 0.1).
source: Analyses between the normalized CHC quantity and desiccation resistance showed no correlation between these two variables in males (Male: p = 0.1) and positive correlation in females (Female: r = 0.1, p = 0.03) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on Pearson correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is a weak positive correlation between normalized CHC quantity and desiccation resistance in females (r = 0.1, p = 0.03).
source: Analyses between the normalized CHC quantity and desiccation resistance showed no correlation between these two variables in males (Male: p = 0.1) and positive correlation in females (Female: r = 0.1, p = 0.03) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on Pearson correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Having higher amounts of CHCs only have a limited contribution to higher desiccation resistance.
source: The low value of r (0.1) indicates a weak correlation between CHC quantities and desiccation resistance in females. This suggests that having higher amounts of CHCs only have a limited contribution to higher desiccation resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the weak correlation coefficient (r = 0.1) observed in the data analysis.

claim: The beta diversity of CHC compositions differs significantly across increasing desiccation resistance (r2 = 0.1, p < 0.001).
source: Our results showed that the beta diversity of CHC compositions differs significantly across the increasing desiccation resistance (r2 = 0.1, p < 0.001; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that CHC composition is important for desiccation resistance.
evidence: This is based on PERMANOVA analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Random forest modeling of CHC composition was able to explain 85.5% of the variation in desiccation resistance (RMSE = 4.5).
source: Random forest modeling of CHC composition was able to explain 85.5% of the variation in desiccation resistance (out of bag estimate: root mean square error 'RMSE' = 4.5) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on random forest regression analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Four mbCHCs (2MeC30, 2MeC28, 2MeC32, and 2MeC26) were identified as having the highest contribution to predicting desiccation resistance.
source: Four mbCHCs were identified as having the highest contribution to predicting desiccation resistance in the regression model (listed in decreasing importance: 2MeC30, 2MeC28, 2MeC32, and 2MeC26), while many other CHCs did not substantially contribute to predicting desiccation resistance (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on random forest regression analysis showing variable importance in Figure 4B.

claim: The quantity of 2MeC26 negatively correlates with desiccation resistance in males (r = −0.4, p < 0.001).
source: We found that the quantity of 2MeC26 negatively correlates with desiccation resistance in males (r = −0.4, p < 0.001) but no significant correlation was identified in females (p = 0.1) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on Pearson correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There is no significant correlation between the quantity of 2MeC26 and desiccation resistance in females (p = 0.1).
source: We found that the quantity of 2MeC26 negatively correlates with desiccation resistance in males (r = −0.4, p < 0.001) but no significant correlation was identified in females (p = 0.1) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on Pearson correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Significant positive correlations were observed between quantities of 2MeC28 and desiccation resistance for females (r = 0.4, p < 0.001) and males (r = 0.4, p < 0.001).
source: Significant positive correlations were observed between quantities of the longer mbCHCs and desiccation resistance for females (2MeC28: r = 0.4, p < 0.001; 2MeC30: r = 0.2, p = 0.009; 2MeC32: r = 0.3, p < 0.001) and males (2MeC28: r = 0.4, p < 0.001; 2MeC32: r = 0.4, p < 0.001) (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is based on Pearson correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Significant positive correlation was observed between quantity of 2MeC30 and desiccation resistance in females (r = 0.2, p = 0.009).
source: Significant positive correlations were observed between quantities of the longer mbCHCs and desiccation resistance for females (2MeC28: r = 0.4, p < 0.001; 2MeC30: r = 0.2, p = 0.009; 2MeC32: r = 0.3, p < 0.001) and males (2MeC28: r = 0.4, p < 0.001; 2MeC32: r = 0.4, p < 0.001) (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is based on Pearson correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Significant positive correlation was observed between quantity of 2MeC32 and desiccation resistance for females (r = 0.3, p < 0.001) and males (r = 0.4, p < 0.001).
source: Significant positive correlations were observed between quantities of the longer mbCHCs and desiccation resistance for females (2MeC28: r = 0.4, p < 0.001; 2MeC30: r = 0.2, p = 0.009; 2MeC32: r = 0.3, p < 0.001) and males (2MeC28: r = 0.4, p < 0.001; 2MeC32: r = 0.4, p < 0.001) (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is based on Pearson correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No significant correlation was observed between quantity of 2MeC30 and desiccation resistance in males.
source: However, no significant correlation was observed between quantity of 2MeC30 and desiccation resistance in males (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on Pearson correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Coating of 2MeC26 did not increase desiccation resistance in both sexes of D. melanogaster (Female: p = 0.07; Male: p = 1.0).
source: Our desiccation assays showed that the coating of 2MeC26 did not increase desiccation resistance in both sexes (post hoc comparison with Tukey's method followed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). Female: p = 0.07; Male: p = 1.0), while 2MeC30 significantly increased desiccation resistance in female D. melanogaster (t = 11.2, p < 0.001), and both 2MeC28 (t = 4.6, p < 0.001) and 2MeC30 (t = 6.9, p < 0.001) significantly increased desiccation resistance in male D. melanogaster (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on experimental desiccation assays with synthetic CHC coating shown in Figure 5E.

claim: 2MeC30 significantly increased desiccation resistance in female D. melanogaster (t = 11.2, p < 0.001).
source: Our desiccation assays showed that the coating of 2MeC26 did not increase desiccation resistance in both sexes (post hoc comparison with Tukey's method followed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). Female: p = 0.07; Male: p = 1.0), while 2MeC30 significantly increased desiccation resistance in female D. melanogaster (t = 11.2, p < 0.001), and both 2MeC28 (t = 4.6, p < 0.001) and 2MeC30 (t = 6.9, p < 0.001) significantly increased desiccation resistance in male D. melanogaster (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on experimental desiccation assays with synthetic CHC coating shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Both 2MeC28 (t = 4.6, p < 0.001) and 2MeC30 (t = 6.9, p < 0.001) significantly increased desiccation resistance in male D. melanogaster.
source: Our desiccation assays showed that the coating of 2MeC26 did not increase desiccation resistance in both sexes (post hoc comparison with Tukey's method followed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). Female: p = 0.07; Male: p = 1.0), while 2MeC30 significantly increased desiccation resistance in female D. melanogaster (t = 11.2, p < 0.001), and both 2MeC28 (t = 4.6, p < 0.001) and 2MeC30 (t = 6.9, p < 0.001) significantly increased desiccation resistance in male D. melanogaster (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on experimental desiccation assays with synthetic CHC coating shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There is a positive correlation between longer mbCHC length coated and higher desiccation resistance.
source: There is a positive correlation with longer mbCHC length coated and higher desiccation resistance (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that having higher quantities of longer mbCHCs can lead to higher desiccation resistance.
evidence: This is based on Pearson correlation analysis of experimental coating data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Coating with n-alkanes on the attP40 strain led to increases in desiccation resistance, which is positively correlated with carbon-chain length.
source: Coating with n-alkanes on the attP40 strain led to increases in desiccation resistance, which is positively correlated with carbon-chain length, similar to the mbCHCs experiments, suggesting that longer chain CHCs, with higher melting temperatures, can confer higher desiccation resistance when coated on the attP40 strain (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on experimental desiccation assays with synthetic n-alkane coating shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and 4.

claim: Phylogenetic signals in mbCHCs were detected for both females and males with λ = 0.75 and 0.83, respectively.
source: Phylogenetic signals in mbCHCs were detected for both females and males with λ = 0.75 and 0.83, respectively (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is based on Pagel's λ analysis of phylogenetic signal in the data.

claim: The derived ancestral state for mbCHCs in the Drosophila genus suggest that 2MeC28 and 2MeC30 are the major mbCHCs.
source: The derived ancestral state for mbCHCs in the Drosophila genus suggest that 2MeC28 and 2MeC30 are the major mbCHCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on ancestral trait reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Independent evolution of longer mbCHCs was observed in four clades of species, including the willistoni, nasuta, and repleta groups, and the ananassae subgroup.
source: Independent evolution of longer mbCHCs was observed in four clades of species, including the willistoni, nasuta, and repleta groups, and the ananassae subgroup (including D. ananassae, D. pseudoananassae, and D. bipectinata), while shorter mbCHCs were mainly observed in several species in the melanogaster subgroup (e.g., D. melanogaster, D. simulans, and D. teissieri) (Figure 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on ancestral trait reconstruction and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Shorter mbCHCs were mainly observed in several species in the melanogaster subgroup (e.g., D. melanogaster, D. simulans, and D. teissieri).
source: Independent evolution of longer mbCHCs was observed in four clades of species, including the willistoni, nasuta, and repleta groups, and the ananassae subgroup (including D. ananassae, D. pseudoananassae, and D. bipectinata), while shorter mbCHCs were mainly observed in several species in the melanogaster subgroup (e.g., D. melanogaster, D. simulans, and D. teissieri) (Figure 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on ancestral trait reconstruction and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: After correcting for phylogenetic effects, the higher quantity and longer length of the longest mbCHC both affect desiccation resistance (interaction term, Female: t = 3.5, p < 0.001; Male: t = 2.2, p = 0.03).
source: PGLS modeling showed, after correcting for phylogenetic effects, the higher quantity and longer length of the longest mbCHC both affect desiccation resistance (interaction term, Female: t = 3.5, p < 0.001; Male: t = 2.2, p = 0.03) (Supplementary file 1c; Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on Phylogenetic Generalized Linear Square (PGLS) analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: CHC composition can account for 85.5% of the variation in desiccation resistance in the 50 Drosophila and related species.
source: We showed that CHC composition can account for 85.5% of the variation in desiccation resistance in the 50 Drosophila and related species in this study.
evidence: This is based on random forest regression analysis of experimental data.

claim: Cuticular water loss is the leading cause of desiccation in insects.
source: In insects, cuticular water loss is the leading cause of desiccation (Chown et al., 2011; Gibbs and Matzkin, 2001; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cuticular water transpiration accounts for 97% of increased water loss in queens of the harvester ant Pogonomyrmex barbatus.
source: In an extreme example, cuticular water transpiration has been found to account for 97% of increased water loss in queens of the harvester ant Pogonomyrmex barbatus (Johnson and Gibbs, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research by Johnson and Gibbs, 2004.

claim: The CHC layer can contain more than 100 different compounds on the same individual.
source: This CHC layer, which can contain more than 100 different compounds on the same individual, provides a hydrophobic barrier against evaporative water loss through the cuticle (Blomquist and Ginzel, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research by Blomquist and Ginzel, 2021.

claim: Physical or chemical removal of the CHC layer using abrasive dust and various solvents resulted in increased water loss in various insect species.
source: This was first demonstrated when the physical or chemical removal of this layer using abrasive dust and various solvents resulted in increased water loss in various insect species in experiments published almost eight decades ago (Wigglesworth, 1945).
evidence: This is supported by citation to historical research by Wigglesworth, 1945.

claim: Genetic manipulations of the cytochrome P450 decarbonylase gene in D. melanogaster, aphids, and cockroaches led to almost complete loss of CHCs and significant decrease in desiccation resistance.
source: In recent years, after the identification of a cytochrome P450 decarbonylase responsible for the synthesis of insect CHCs (Qiu et al., 2012), genetic manipulations of this gene in the fruitfly Drosophila melanogaster as well as in aphids and cockroaches, led to almost complete loss of CHCs and significant decrease in desiccation resistance (Chen et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019; Qiu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Qiu et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019).

claim: The melting temperature of the hydrocarbon is positively correlated with its water-proofing properties and contribution to desiccation resistance.
source: The melting temperature of the hydrocarbon is positively correlated with its water-proofing properties and contribution to desiccation resistance (Blomquist and Ginzel, 2021; Gibbs and Rajpurohit, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Blomquist and Ginzel, 2021; Gibbs and Rajpurohit, 2010).

claim: Increase in CHC chain length can increase melting temperature and potentially leads to higher desiccation resistance.
source: Increase in CHC chain length can also increase melting temperature and potentially leads to higher desiccation resistance (Gibbs and Pomonis, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research by Gibbs and Pomonis, 1995.

claim: Laboratory selection experiments in D. melanogaster selecting for increased desiccation resistance resulted in longer carbon-chain CHCs in the desiccation selected flies than the control flies.
source: This is consistent with laboratory selection experiments in D. melanogaster selecting for increased desiccation resistance resulted in longer carbon-chain CHCs in the desiccation selected flies than the control flies (Gibbs et al., 1997; Kwan and Rundle, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Gibbs et al., 1997; Kwan and Rundle, 2010).

claim: Longer CHC chain length is correlated with climatic factors such as higher temperature and lower precipitation.
source: Longer CHC chain length is also correlated with climatic factors such as higher temperature and lower precipitation (Jezovit et al., 2017; Rouault et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Jezovit et al., 2017; Rouault et al., 2004).

claim: A cohort-based experimental design was used where subsets of each cohort were used for GC–MS determination of CHC profiles, desiccation resistance assays, and measuring body weight.
source: As the assays for CHCs and desiccation resistance cannot be performed on the same individuals, we used a cohort-based experimental design (Figure 1) where subsets of each cohort (5–6 per species) were used for gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) determination of CHC profiles, desiccation resistance assays, and measuring body weight of the F1 progeny for each sex.
evidence: This is described in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: All measurements were performed at the cohort level.
source: Therefore, all measurements were performed at the cohort level.
evidence: This is stated in the experimental design description.

claim: The 46 Drosophila species represent some of the main groups in the Drosophila genus: melanogaster group, obscura group, willistoni group, nasuta group, virilis group, and repleta group.
source: The 46 Drosophila species represent some of the main groups in the Drosophila genus: (1) melanogaster group, (2) obscura group, (3) willistoni group, (4) nasuta group, (5) virilis group, and (6) repleta group.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The integration of peak areas on longer CHCs is biased to have lower values in GC-MS analysis.
source: The integration of peak areas on longer cuticular hydrocarbons (CHCs) is biased to have lower values. To address this issue, we corrected the peak areas of CHCs based on the carbon-chain lengths using the integration from this standard n-alkane mixture.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and described in the Materials and methods.

claim: n-Alkanes are only present in some species from the melanogaster group.
source: n-Alkanes are only present in some species from the melanogaster group.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2 and shown in the figure.

claim: All CHCs are synthesized via the fatty acyl-CoA synthesis pathway from acetyl-CoA.
source: All CHCs are synthesized via the fatty acyl-CoA synthesis pathway from acetyl-CoA. The pathway splits early due to the action of two fatty acid synthetases (FAS) into the branched CHC pathway or the linear CHC pathway.
evidence: This is described in the caption of Figure 5—figure supplement 8 and is based on established knowledge of CHC biosynthesis pathways.

claim: The pathway splits early due to the action of two fatty acid synthetases (FAS) into the branched CHC pathway or the linear CHC pathway.
source: All CHCs are synthesized via the fatty acyl-CoA synthesis pathway from acetyl-CoA. The pathway splits early due to the action of two fatty acid synthetases (FAS) into the branched CHC pathway or the linear CHC pathway.
evidence: This is described in the caption of Figure 5—figure supplement 8 and is based on established knowledge of CHC biosynthesis pathways.

claim: CHC- D. melanogaster flies are generated by crossing 5′mFAS-GAL4 and UAS-Cyp4g1-RNAi, resulting in adult oenocyte specific knockdown of Cyp4g1 and loss of CHC production.
source: CHC- D. melanogaster flies are generated by crossing 5′mFAS-GAL4 and UAS-Cyp4g1-RNAi, resulting in adult oenocyte specific knockdown of Cyp4g1 and loss of cuticular hydrocarbon (CHC) production.
evidence: This is described in the caption of Figure 5—figure supplement 9 and in the Materials and methods section.

claim: cVA (cis-vaccenyl acetate) is a lipid produced in the male ejaculatory bulb not affected by the RNAi knockdown of Cyp4g1 in the oenocytes.
source: cVA = cis-vaccenyl acetate, a lipid produced in the male ejaculatory bulb not affected by the RNAi knockdown of Cyp4g1 in the oenocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 5—figure supplement 9.

claim: Desiccation resistance differences across Drosophila species can be largely explained by variations in cuticular hydrocarbons.
source: Desiccation resistance differences in Drosophila species can be largely explained by variations in cuticular hydrocarbons
evidence: This is the main title of the manuscript and is supported by the overall findings of the study.

claim: Length variation in methyl-branched CHCs (mbCHCs) is a key determinant of desiccation resistance.
source: In particular, length variation in a subset of CHCs, the methyl-branched CHCs (mbCHCs), is a key determinant of desiccation resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract and is supported by the random forest analysis and correlation studies.

claim: There is a significant correlation between the evolution of longer mbCHCs and higher desiccation resistance in these species.
source: There is also a significant correlation between the evolution of longer mbCHCs and higher desiccation resistance in these species.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract and is supported by the PGLS analysis.

claim: Evolutionary changes in insect CHC components can be a general mechanism for the evolution of desiccation resistance and adaptation to diverse and changing environments.
source: Given that CHCs are almost ubiquitous in insects, we suggest that evolutionary changes in insect CHC components can be a general mechanism for the evolution of desiccation resistance and adaptation to diverse and changing environments.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract and represents a broader inference from the study's findings.

claim: Insects have a high surface area to volume ratio due to their small sizes, rendering them vulnerable to water loss and desiccation.
source: Organisms such as insects have a high surface area to volume ratio due to their small sizes, rendering them vulnerable to water loss and desiccation (Gibbs, 2002b; Gibbs and Rajpurohit, 2010; Kühsel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Phylogenetically related insect species can have very different levels of desiccation resistance and occupy very distinct habitats.
source: Studies using closely related insect species collected worldwide showed that phylogenetically related insect species can have very different levels of desiccation resistance and occupy very distinct habitats, while insects that are phylogenetically distant but dwelling in similar habitats could have similar levels of desiccation resistance (Kellermann et al., 2012; Li et al., 2022; Menzel et al., 2017; Rane et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous research (Kellermann et al., 2012; Li et al., 2022; Menzel et al., 2017; Rane et al., 2019).

claim: Insects that are phylogenetically distant but dwelling in similar habitats could have similar levels of desiccation resistance.
source: Studies using closely related insect species collected worldwide showed that phylogenetically related insect species can have very different levels of desiccation resistance and occupy very distinct habitats, while insects that are phylogenetically distant but dwelling in similar habitats could have similar levels of desiccation resistance (Kellermann et al., 2012; Li et al., 2022; Menzel et al., 2017; Rane et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous research (Kellermann et al., 2012; Li et al., 2022; Menzel et al., 2017; Rane et al., 2019).

claim: Climate change is accelerating the expansion of dryland.
source: However, as climate change accelerates the expansion of dryland (Huang et al., 2016) and changes aridity in many areas across the globe (Sherwood and Fu, 2014; Shi et al., 2021), it is less understood how insect species, which are integral parts of our ecosystems, can evolve higher levels of desiccation resistance to adapt to the more arid environments.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citation to previous research (Huang et al., 2016).

claim: Climate change is changing aridity in many areas across the globe.
source: However, as climate change accelerates the expansion of dryland (Huang et al., 2016) and changes aridity in many areas across the globe (Sherwood and Fu, 2014; Shi et al., 2021), it is less understood how insect species, which are integral parts of our ecosystems, can evolve higher levels of desiccation resistance to adapt to the more arid environments.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous research (Sherwood and Fu, 2014; Shi et al., 2021).

claim: Variations in the composition of the CHC layer have been suggested to contribute to intraspecific variation in desiccation resistance in D. melanogaster.
source: Variations in the composition of this CHC layer have been suggested to contribute to intraspecific variation in desiccation resistance in D. melanogaster (Rouault et al., 2004), the Mediterranean dung beetle Onthophagus taurus (Leeson et al., 2020), and the Argentine ant Linepithema humile (Buellesbach et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citation to previous research (Rouault et al., 2004).

claim: Variations in the composition of the CHC layer have been suggested to contribute to intraspecific variation in desiccation resistance in the Mediterranean dung beetle Onthophagus taurus.
source: Variations in the composition of this CHC layer have been suggested to contribute to intraspecific variation in desiccation resistance in D. melanogaster (Rouault et al., 2004), the Mediterranean dung beetle Onthophagus taurus (Leeson et al., 2020), and the Argentine ant Linepithema humile (Buellesbach et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citation to previous research (Leeson et al., 2020).

claim: Variations in the composition of the CHC layer have been suggested to contribute to intraspecific variation in desiccation resistance in the Argentine ant Linepithema humile.
source: Variations in the composition of this CHC layer have been suggested to contribute to intraspecific variation in desiccation resistance in D. melanogaster (Rouault et al., 2004), the Mediterranean dung beetle Onthophagus taurus (Leeson et al., 2020), and the Argentine ant Linepithema humile (Buellesbach et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citation to previous research (Buellesbach et al., 2018).

claim: Studies manipulating CHC composition either chemically or genetically in different Drosophila species produced different levels of desiccation resistance.
source: This is supported by studies manipulating CHC composition either chemically or genetically, in different Drosophila species, producing different levels of desiccation resistance (Chiang et al., 2016; Ferveur et al., 2018; Chung et al., 2014; Koto et al., 2019; Savage et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citations to previous research (Chiang et al., 2016; Ferveur et al., 2018; Chung et al., 2014; Koto et al., 2019; Savage et al., 2021).

claim: In Drosophila and most other insects, CHCs range in lengths between approximately 21 and 50 carbons.
source: In Drosophila and most other insects, CHCs range in lengths between approximately 21 and 50 carbons, and consist of linear alkanes (n-alkanes), alkenes (monoenes and dienes), and methyl-branched alkanes (mbCHCs) (Blomquist and Ginzel, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is supported by citation to previous research (Blomquist and Ginzel, 2021).

claim: Among CHC types, n-alkanes have the highest melting temperature, followed by mbCHCs, monoenes, and dienes.
source: Among them, n-alkanes have the highest melting temperature, followed by mbCHCs , monoenes, and dienes.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is based on established knowledge of CHC chemical properties.

claim: RNAi knockdown of a methyl-branched specific fatty acid synthase (mFAS) in D. serrata eliminates almost all mbCHCs and leads to significant decrease in desiccation resistance.
source: RNAi knockdown of a methyl-branched specific fatty acid synthase (mFAS) in D. serrata eliminates almost all mbCHCs and leads to significant decrease in desiccation resistance which could be partially rescued with synthetic mbCHCs (Chung et al., 2014) .
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citation to previous research (Chung et al., 2014).

claim: D. birchii have only trace amounts of mbCHCs.
source: Its sibling species, the rainforest desiccation sensitive D. birchii, have only trace amounts of mbCHCs (Howard et al., 2003) and is unable to evolve desiccation resistance despite strong laboratory selection over many generations (Hoffmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citation to previous research (Howard et al., 2003).

claim: D. birchii is unable to evolve desiccation resistance despite strong laboratory selection over many generations.
source: Its sibling species, the rainforest desiccation sensitive D. birchii, have only trace amounts of mbCHCs (Howard et al., 2003) and is unable to evolve desiccation resistance despite strong laboratory selection over many generations (Hoffmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citation to previous research (Hoffmann et al., 2003).

claim: A high proportion of very-long-chain mbCHCs with a single methyl branch have been reported in many insect species from different taxa that dwell in desert environments.
source: A high proportion of very-long-chain mbCHCs with a single methyl branch have been reported in many insect species from different taxa that dwell in desert environments, such as the desert tenebrionid beetle Eleodes armata (Hadley, 1977), the desert ants Cataglyphis niger and P. barbatus (Johnson and Gibbs, 2004; Soroker and Hefetz, 2000), and the desert locust Schistocerca gregaria (Heifetz et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous research (Hadley, 1977; Johnson and Gibbs, 2004; Soroker and Hefetz, 2000; Heifetz et al., 1998).

claim: The use of mbCHCs to minimize water evaporation may be a common mechanism for insects in extremely dry environments.
source: Although a small proportion of n-alkanes was also reported in some of these species, this suggests the use of mbCHCs to minimize water evaporation may be a common mechanism for insects in extremely dry environments.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that many desert-dwelling insect species have high proportions of mbCHCs.

claim: The ability to synthesize longer mbCHCs may be lost during evolution, especially for species that do not inhabit arid environments and have low levels of desiccation resistance.
source: As there are many extant species that do not have 2MeC30, this suggests that the ability to synthesize longer mbCHCs may be lost during evolution, especially for species that do not inhabit arid environments and have low levels of desiccation resistance such as D. melanogaster and D. biarmipes.
evidence: This is inferred from the ancestral trait reconstruction showing 2MeC30 as ancestral but absent in some extant species.

claim: For species that dwell in extremely arid environments such as D. mojavensis and D. arizonae, higher quantities of 2MeC30 and an even longer mbCHC, 2MeC32, are observed.
source: On the contrary, for species that dwell in extremely arid environments such as D. mojavensis and D. arizonae, higher quantities of 2MeC30 and an even longer mbCHC, 2MeC32, are observed.
evidence: This is based on the CHC analysis data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 6.

claim: The synthesis of n-alkanes, monoenes, and dienes are in competition in the CHC biosynthesis pathway.
source: The pathway is split where a cytosolic fatty acid synthase (cFAS) will synthesize all the linear CHCs (n-alkanes, monoenes, dienes), while mFAS will synthesize mbCHCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 8; Chung and Carroll, 2015; Holze et al., 2021). The pathway suggests that the synthesis of n-alkanes, monoenes, and dienes are in competition.
evidence: This is inferred from the CHC biosynthesis pathway diagram shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 8 and supported by citations (Chung and Carroll, 2015; Holze et al., 2021).

claim: Many monoenes and dienes function in Drosophila as contact pheromones in regulating different behaviors such as mating and aggression.
source: As many monoenes and dienes function in Drosophila as contact pheromones in regulating different behaviors such as mating and aggression (Blomquist and Ginzel, 2021; Chertemps et al., 2007; Chertemps et al., 2006; Chung and Carroll, 2015; Krupp et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011), the synthesis for these CHCs may compete with the synthesis of n-alkanes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous research (Blomquist and Ginzel, 2021; Chertemps et al., 2007; Chertemps et al., 2006; Chung and Carroll, 2015; Krupp et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011).

claim: The synthesis of mbCHCs is relatively unaffected by other products of the CHC biosynthesis pathway.
source: In contrast, the synthesis of mbCHCs is in another part of the pathway. This suggests that there are potential constraints in the roles of n-alkanes in desiccation resistance in Drosophila due to competition with CHCs which function as signaling molecules, while the synthesis of mbCHCs is relatively unaffected by other products of the pathway (Figure 5—figure supplement 8; Chung and Carroll, 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the CHC biosynthesis pathway diagram shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 8 and supported by citation (Chung and Carroll, 2015).

claim: In D. serrata, having higher amounts of 2MeC26 leads to higher mating success in male D. serrata.
source: In D. serrata, having higher amounts of 2MeC26 leads to higher mating success in male D. serrata (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citation to previous research (Chung et al., 2014).

claim: Northern populations of D. serrata produce lower amounts of 2MeC26 but higher amounts of 2MeC30, due to a polymorphism in a fatty acyl-CoA reductase gene.
source: Northern populations of this species produce lower amounts of 2MeC26 but higher amounts of 2MeC30, due to a polymorphism in a fatty acyl-CoA reductase gene that shifts to an overall production of longer CHCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citation to previous research (Rusuwa et al., 2022).

claim: The polymorphism in D. serrata led to lower mating success in male northern flies and higher desiccation resistance in female northern flies compared to their common counterparts.
source: As CHCs are sexually monomorphic in D. serrata, this polymorphism led to lower mating success in male northern flies and higher desiccation resistance in female northern flies compared to their common counterparts (Rusuwa et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citation to previous research (Rusuwa et al., 2022).

claim: Diet can affect CHC profiles in D. melanogaster.
source: Previous studies have shown that diet (Fedina et al., 2012), temperature (Rajpurohit et al., 2021), and mating status (Everaerts et al., 2010) can affect CHC profiles in D. melanogaster, therefore the CHC profiles that we obtained in our studies may not be representative of the CHC variations present in some of these species in their natural habitats.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citation to previous research (Fedina et al., 2012).

claim: Temperature can affect CHC profiles in D. melanogaster.
source: Previous studies have shown that diet (Fedina et al., 2012), temperature (Rajpurohit et al., 2021), and mating status (Everaerts et al., 2010) can affect CHC profiles in D. melanogaster, therefore the CHC profiles that we obtained in our studies may not be representative of the CHC variations present in some of these species in their natural habitats.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citation to previous research (Rajpurohit et al., 2021).

claim: Mating status can affect CHC profiles in D. melanogaster.
source: Previous studies have shown that diet (Fedina et al., 2012), temperature (Rajpurohit et al., 2021), and mating status (Everaerts et al., 2010) can affect CHC profiles in D. melanogaster, therefore the CHC profiles that we obtained in our studies may not be representative of the CHC variations present in some of these species in their natural habitats.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citation to previous research (Everaerts et al., 2010).

claim: CHC variations between different natural populations of the same Drosophila species are largely quantitative than qualitative.
source: Similarly, CHC variations between different natural populations of the same Drosophila species are also largely quantitative than qualitative (Dembeck et al., 2015; Rusuwa et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citations to previous research (Dembeck et al., 2015; Rusuwa et al., 2022).

claim: In Lepidoptera, volatile non-CHC pheromones are predominantly used for chemical communication.
source: In other insect orders such as Lepidoptera, where volatile non-CHC pheromones are predominantly used for chemical communication (Ando et al., 2004), constraints on each class of CHCs may be different from Drosophila.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citation to previous research (Ando et al., 2004).

claim: Across eusocial hymenopterans, saturated CHCs such as n-alkanes and mbCHCs are used as queen pheromones.
source: Likewise, across eusocial hymenopterans (Van Oystaeyen et al., 2014), saturated CHCs such as n-alkanes and mbCHCs are used as queen pheromones and are likely to be under constraints in the evolution of desiccation resistance in these species.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citation to previous research (Van Oystaeyen et al., 2014).

claim: In dragonflies, very-long-chain methyl ketones and aldehydes are the major cuticular wax components.
source: Finally, in some rare examples such as dragonflies where very-long-chain methyl ketones and aldehydes are the major cuticular wax components (Futahashi et al., 2019), the evolution of CHCs may not be a major factor in the evolution of desiccation resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by citation to previous research (Futahashi et al., 2019).

claim: The synthesis of mbCHCs with longer carbon-chain lengths is a common mechanism underlying the evolution of higher desiccation resistance in Drosophila.
source: While we limit our conclusions that the synthesis of mbCHCs with longer carbon-chain lengths is a common mechanism underlying the evolution of higher desiccation resistance to Drosophila, the evolution of cuticular components that modulate the melting temperature of the cuticular lipid layer can reduce water loss and increase desiccation resistance.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental data and analyses.

claim: The evolution of cuticular components that modulate the melting temperature of the cuticular lipid layer can reduce water loss and increase desiccation resistance.
source: While we limit our conclusions that the synthesis of mbCHCs with longer carbon-chain lengths is a common mechanism underlying the evolution of higher desiccation resistance to Drosophila, the evolution of cuticular components that modulate the melting temperature of the cuticular lipid layer can reduce water loss and increase desiccation resistance.
evidence: This is a broader generalization inferred from the study's findings.

claim: The evolution of CHC components in insects can be largely predictive of desiccation resistance between closely related species.
source: We suggest that the evolution of CHC components in insects can be largely predictive of desiccation resistance between closely related species.
evidence: This is the final conclusion of the Discussion section based on the study's findings.

claim: All species were reared on standard cornmeal medium.
source: All species were reared on standard cornmeal medium (Flystuff 66-121 Nutri-Fly Bloomington Formulation).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The phylogenetic relationship of all 50 species in this study was adapted from Finet et al., 2021.
source: The phylogenetic relationship of all 50 species in this study was adapted from Finet et al., 2021.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: For each species, five to six cohorts were established by pooling five females and five males on a standard cornmeal medium at 25°C and a 12L:12D photoperiod.
source: For each species, five to six cohorts were established and three measurements were conducted for each sex of the F1 progeny, including desiccation resistance, CHCs, and body weight (Figure 1). Each cohort was treated as a biological replicate. Each cohort in each species was established by pooling five females and five males on a standard cornmeal medium in the environmental chambers set at 25°C and a 12L:12D photoperiod.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: F1 progeny flies were collected daily following emergence, separated by sex, and maintained on fresh cornmeal medium.
source: F1 progeny flies were collected daily following emergence, separated by sex, and maintained on fresh cornmeal medium.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All flies used for measurements were 4- to 5-day old.
source: All flies used for measurements were 4- to 5-day old.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Desiccation resistance assays were performed in a randomized and blinded manner.
source: Desiccation resistance assays were performed in a randomized and blinded manner with the setup consistent with a previously published protocol (Figure 1; Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In each cohort, 10 adults of the same sex were subjected to the desiccation assay setup containing 10 g of silica gel.
source: Briefly, in each cohort, 10 adults of the same sex were subjected to the assay setup containing 10 g of silica gel (S7500-1KG, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Mortality of the flies was recorded hourly after 2 hr in desiccation assays.
source: Mortality of the flies was recorded hourly after 2 hr.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: CHCs were extracted by soaking five flies in 200 µl hexane containing hexacosane (C26; 25 ng/µl) as an internal standard for 10 min.
source: Five flies of the same sex (4- to 5-day old) from each cohort were soaked for 10 min in 200 µl hexane containing hexacosane (C26; 25 ng/µl) as an internal standard.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: CHC extracts were analyzed by GC–MS using a DB-17ht column.
source: Extracts were directly analyzed by GC–MS (7890A, Agilent Technologies Inc, Santa Clara, CA) using a DB-17ht column (Agilent Technologies Inc, Santa Clara, CA).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The types of CHCs were identified by a combination of their specific fragment ions, retention times relative to linear hydrocarbon standards, and the m/z value of the molecular ion.
source: The types of CHCs, including methyl-branched alkanes, monoenes, dienes, and trienes, were then identified by a combination of their specific fragment ions on the side of functional groups (methyl branch or double bonds), retention times relative to linear hydrocarbon standards, and the m/z value of the molecular ion.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The position of methyl branch in mbCHCs was determined using the protocol described in Carlson et al., 1998.
source: The position of methyl branch in mbCHCs was determined using the protocol described in Carlson et al., 1998, while the position of double bonds was not determined in this study.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The position of double bonds in CHCs was not determined in this study.
source: The position of methyl branch in mbCHCs was determined using the protocol described in Carlson et al., 1998, while the position of double bonds was not determined in this study.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Each CHC peak was quantified using its comparison with the peak area of the internal standard (C26) and represented as nanogram per fly (ng/fly).
source: Each CHC peak was quantified using its comparison with the peak area of the internal standard (C26) and represented as nanogram per fly (ng/fly).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The peak areas of CHCs were corrected based on the carbon-chain lengths using the integration from the standard mixture.
source: Because we observed a biased integration of peak areas on longer CHCs in running the standard mixture (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we corrected the peak areas of CHCs based on the carbon-chain lengths using the integration from the standard mixture.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Body weight was determined as the difference between the Eppendorf tube containing 5–10 flies of the same sex and the same empty Eppendorf tube.
source: The body weight was determined as the difference between the Eppendorf tube containing 5–10 flies of the same sex and the same empty Eppendorf tube.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: To coat synthetic CHCs on D. melanogaster, 200 µl hexane containing 300 ng/µl of each CHC was added to a 2-ml glass vial and hexane was evaporated.
source: To coat each of synthetic mbCHCs and n-alkanes on D. melanogaster, including 2MeC26, 2MeC28, 2MeC30, C23, C25, C27, C29, and C31, we first added 200 µl hexane containing 300 ng/µl of each CHC in a 2-ml glass vial and then used a nitrogen evaporator (BT1603 G-Biosciences) to evaporate the hexane with only mbCHCs precipitate at the bottom of the vial.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: After hexane evaporation, 10 flies were transferred into each vial and shaken on a Vortex for 20 s on, 20 s off, and 20 s on.
source: After the hexane was evaporated, 10 flies of the same sex were transferred into each vial, following shaking on a Vortex for 20 s on, 20 s off, and 20 s on, following previous protocols (Billeter et al., 2009; Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Synthetic mbCHCs were kindly provided by Dr. Jocelyn Millar (University of California, Riverside).
source: Synthetic mbCHCs were kindly provided by Dr. Jocelyn Millar (University of California, Riverside) and synthetic n-alkanes were ordered from Sigma-Aldrich (C23 #91447-1G, C25 #286931-1G, C27 #51559-250MG, C29 #74156-250MG, and C31 #51529-250MG).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.1).
source: All analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.1).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Correlation analyses were conducted with Pearson's method using 'cor.test' function.
source: Correlation analyses were conducted with Pearson's method using 'cor.test' function.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Variance in CHC beta diversity across desiccation resistance was determined using PERMANOVA using the 'vegan' package.
source: Variance in CHC beta diversity across desiccation resistance was determined using PERMANOVA using the 'vegan' package (Anderson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The random forest regression analysis was performed using the 'ranger' and 'randomForest' packages.
source: The random forest regression analysis was performed using the 'ranger' and 'randomForest' packages (Liaw and Wiener, 2002; Wright and Ziegler, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The importance of top predictor CHCs was quantified using permutation importance.
source: To determine how useful each CHC variable is in the prediction of desiccation resistance in the random forest regression analysis, the importance of top predictor CHCs was quantified using permutation importance (Altmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Desiccation resistance in flies coated with different mbCHCs was determined using one-way ANOVA at alpha = 0.05.
source: Desiccation resistance in flies coated with different mbCHCs was determined using one-way ANOVA at alpha = 0.05. Post hoc comparison was further conducted using Tukey's method.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The ancestral trait reconstruction and estimation of phylogenetic signal, Pagel's λ, were determined using 'Phytools', 'Picante', and 'Rphylopars' packages.
source: The ancestral trait reconstruction and estimation of phylogenetic signal, Pagel's λ, for mbCHC composition and desiccation resistance were determined using 'Phytools', 'Picante', and 'Rphylopars' packages (Goolsby et al., 2017; Kembel et al., 2010; Revell, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The PGLS analysis was conducted using generalized least squares fit by maximum likelihood and the covariance structure between species was used under a Brownian motion process of evolution.
source: The PGLS analysis was conducted using generalized least squares fit by maximum likelihood and the covariance structure between species was used under a Brownian motion process of evolution. The PGLS analyses were conducted using 'GLS' function in 'ape' package (Paradis and Schliep, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
